match.reason: No bank point covers how genres change over time through adaptation, remakes and new versions; the closest points cover only single subversions or hybrid texts, which are narrower than the brief.

draft.title: How genres change
card: A genre is a group of texts that share conventions, such as the usual characters, settings and plot of a detective story. Genres do not stay fixed. They change as audiences and values change.
Adapted
a genre's conventions are moved into a new form, setting or time. A fairytale might be retold as a film set in a modern city.
Hybrid
conventions from two genres are mixed into one text. A story that is both a western and science fiction is a hybrid.
Subverted
a text sets up a genre's conventions, then twists them on purpose. A fairytale in which the princess rescues herself, and does not marry the prince, subverts the genre.
draft.remember: Genres change as audiences and values change: they can be adapted, mixed or subverted.

a.q: A film uses the usual steps of a murder mystery, but the story is set on a space station and the detective is a robot. What is the film doing with the genre?
opts: Adapting it by moving its conventions to a new setting
Subverting it by twisting its conventions on purpose
Mixing it with a genre that has no conventions
Leaving it unchanged so it matches older versions
a.why: The murder mystery conventions are kept and moved to a new setting, so the genre is adapted. Nothing is turned against audience expectations, so it is not subverted.
a.clue: Are the conventions kept and moved, or turned upside down?

b.q: In a new version of a fairytale, the young hero is expected to defeat the dragon. Instead he befriends it, and the story ends with the dragon teaching him to read. Which statement best describes this change?
opts: It subverts the genre by twisting a convention on purpose
It makes a hybrid by mixing in a second genre's conventions
It adapts the genre by moving it into a new form
It leaves the genre unchanged because a dragon appears
b.why: The story sets up the usual convention of a hero defeating a monster, then twists it on purpose, so it subverts the genre. It is not a hybrid, because no second genre's conventions are mixed in. The form and setting have not changed, so it is not an adaptation.
b.clue: The story builds an expectation, then does the opposite.

a.best: Adapting it by moving its conventions to a new setting

b.best: It subverts the genre by twisting a convention on purpose

problems.detail: A murder mystery set on a space station with a robot detective brings in science-fiction conventions. By the card's own example (a western that is also science fiction is a hybrid), this reads as a hybrid. Teaching it as only an adaptation clashes with the card. The only hybrid option is made absurd ('a genre that has no conventions'), so the question works only by ruling hybrid out artificially. Use a setting that is not genre-marked, such as a modern office or a small town today.

check.summary: Question a's scenario (space station, robot detective) is arguably a mystery/science-fiction hybrid under the card's own definition, so calling it only an adaptation could mislead. Question b and the card are fine.
